Hi Franziska,

Apologies for the late reply (assuming this is following up on a previous post re this question). I will include what I just sent to the previous post here for completeness:

"
Currently, that model does not have model regressors available. Unfortunately, this means that the only way to do it would be to modify the raw stan code to get what you need.

I am not sure when model regressors will generally be available across models—Young may be better suited to answer that than I am at the moment!
"

That said, if you would like to modify the Stan code, you can follow the example in the go/no-go models. e.g., lines 133-137 here show the basic idea: https://github.com/CCS-Lab/hBayesDM/blob/develop/commons/stan_files/gng_m1.stan, where you define variables that will store the values you are interested in. Then, you would need to include a list in the "regressors" argument of the function call (i.e. ts_par6(..., regressors = list(...))) that gives the names and dimensions of the variables of interests (corresponding gng example is here: https://github.com/CCS-Lab/hBayesDM/blob/develop/R/R/gng_m1.R). Additionally, you would need to specify the path to your modified stan model code using the "stanmodel_arg" argument when calling the function (i.e. ts_par6(..., stanmodel_arg = "path_to_stancode.stan")).

This should allow you to extract information of interest—let me know if this is clear!

Best,

Dear all,
we are currently doing some reanalysis for data we have analysed some time ago.
We used gng_m4 for patient data, at the time we modelled means and medians for individual subject parameters. Now, doing a clustering analysis we find that the median parameters classify groups nearly perfectly, while the means provide a poor fit.

If I understand that correctly, the mean and the median simply describes how the parameter is summarised by subject.

If we are thinking of learning rate for example then is it correct to assume that for the mean  this means that from trial to trial the learning rate is being updated based on the mean distribution of the past trials, where as for the median it would be the median distribution? Therefore using the median would (as it always does) take extreme behaviour less into account?

Thank you very much for your help.
Franziska

Hi Franziska,

The mean/median is computed as the mean or median of the posterior distributions for each person. So, it is really just a way to summarize the parameter estimates for each person. In other words, the posterior distribution itself is unchanged whether you use the mean/median argument when fitting (Stan is estimating the full posterior distribution). You could actually compute the posterior means/medians with the fitted model parameters if interested, we only include the argument for convenience.

Let me know if that is clear!

Best,
Nate

I also think it is better to rather emphasize on group parameters than individual parameters, since hBayesDM uses hierarchical model

Best wishes,
Minchul

messages.body_plain:
Hello, Franziska

I am not a statistic person, and my comments can be wrong - I wonder what the hBayesDM developers think.
I mentioned about the group parameters because of the 'Shrinkage' in hierarchical models.
I cannot mathematically prove, but due to shrinkage one's individual parameter estimates would regress toward group mean,
rather than reflecting one's characteristic.
But hierarchical model pools  individual data so this effect makes the group parameter reliable, even though small number of subjects
(I think 30 people is enough to estimate group paratmeter)

For the questions, I think what is important is your theory about the data.
If you think the participants data are drawn from different group parameters, I think you should fit model separately for each groups, vice versa.
OR I think you can fit both hypothesis (one group or two groups) and to Bayesian model comparison to choose winning model.

Best wishes,
Minchul

messages.subject_clean: GNG mean vs median model parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Franziska,

In a hierarchical Bayesian framework, group and individual parameters are estimated simultaneously. For each individual, there's an individual posterior distribution and we can calculate its summary statistics like posterior mean (the mean of a posterior distribution) or posterior median. By default, hBayesDM calculates the means of individual posterior distributions and contain them in 'indPars'.

Hope this helps.

Best,
Young

For each individual, there's an individual posterior distribution and we can calculate its summary statistics like posterior mean (the mean of a posterior distribution) or posterior median. Re computing the prediction errors, I unfortunately do not have a ton of experience with this model and do not currently have the bandwidth to look into it in detail. That said, I can say that what you are saving is the expected value of the choice for the mf controller in your first line, and then the difference in expected value between mf and mb controllers on your second line. To save the prediction error, you would have to take the difference between the realized outcome and the expected value for each controller on that trial.

As for your error message, it may be best to follow what Young described above—that is how you would fully integrate the model with the package. The methods I was describing is a sort of work-around, which seems to be giving trouble. It is hard to say without having the code myself, but I wonder if modifying the ts_par6.r script such that the regressors argument defaults to list("mf_RPE" = 2) would fix it. outputALL_in_6 <- ts_par6(
